strengths: First real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark — a genuine gap in the literature; the paper carefully motivates why LiDAR-based SSC data generation is impractical for UAVs (regulations, payload, sparsity from elevated viewpoints) and fills the void with a large collection (9 scenes, 20,160 samples, 22 classes, ~194,000 m², three altitudes, multiple seasons/scenarios).

The LiDAR-free data generation pipeline (Sec. 3.3) is well-engineered and clearly formalized: SfM+MVS reconstruction, stratified selection of <10% of images for 2D annotation with >99% 3D point coverage (Eq. 3), multi-view label voting with kNN propagation, class-aware densification (visual hull carving for instances, Poisson reconstruction for ground, direct voxelization otherwise), and frustum-culled per-frame ground truth with invalid/surface/occluded masks following SemanticKITTI conventions. The mathematical formulation is precise and reproducible.
Substantial supporting resources: 20k+ metric depth maps, a fine-tuned DAv2-OccuFly depth model, and SSCBench-compatible data organization that eases adoption.

Thorough supplementary material: per-scene reprojection errors, annotation ratios, DBSCAN parameters, class frequencies, depth histograms, scene-level pipeline visualizations (Fig. 10), and a reciprocal cross-domain depth generalization experiment (Tab. 10) that adds scientific value beyond the dataset itself.

Honest limitations section (static scenes, cross-altitude temporal inconsistency, pseudo-label scaling), and useful findings that existing SSC methods (CGFormer) degrade markedly in the aerial regime, motivating future work.
weaknesses: Ground truth validity concerns: since all labels derive from multi-view reconstruction, 'completed' occupancy in occluded regions is fabricated by the pipeline (visual hull filling, Poisson hole-filling) rather than observed; the paper does not quantitatively validate label accuracy against independent reference measurements (e.g., surveyed geometry or manually annotated 3D regions). The claim that densification 'removes such artifacts' (Sec. 4.2) is asserted rather than evidenced. This is a material question for a benchmark whose evaluations hinge on ground-truth quality.

Benchmark breadth is narrow: only one SSC method (CGFormer) is evaluated, and results are extremely low (mIoU 0.008–0.0097, IoU ~0.24–0.29; Tab. 11), with most classes at ~0. This raises unresolved questions about whether the task as posed is learnable, whether the evaluation masks/protocol are misconfigured, or whether label noise dominates — the paper's claim that CGFormer is 'well-suited to aerial SSC under near-uniform class distributions' (Sec. 5.2) contradicts Table 6, which shows extreme imbalance (Building 75.7% vs. Flying Animal 0.0001%).

Geographic and methodological diversity is limited: all 9 scenes come from a single geographic region, and test scenes do not hold out seasons or scenarios (test = Fall/Spring, both present in training), limiting conclusions about generalization.

The depth comparison in Tab. 4 is asymmetric: an in-domain fine-tuned model (DAv2-OccuFly) versus a zero-shot DAv2-metric baseline is not an apples-to-apples comparison, even though the authors partially address this with the reciprocal V-KITTI-2 experiment.

Dataset locations are withheld during review and release is contingent on acceptance, so reproducibility cannot be verified at review time; comparability claims vs. SemanticKITTI (5× samples, 6× voxels) are confounded by very different voxel resolutions (0.5 m vs. 0.2 m) and viewpoints.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: OccuFly is claimed to be the first real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark, and the motivation for avoiding LiDAR on UAVs (mass/energy/regulatory constraints, sparsity from elevated viewpoints) is well argued.

The data generation pipeline (Sec. 3) is carefully formalized and reproducible in spirit: SfM+MVS reconstruction, 2D-to-3D label transfer via multi-view majority voting with kNN refinement, class-aware densification (visual hull carving for instances, Poisson surfaces for ground), frustum culling, and SemanticKITTI-style invalid/surface/occluded masks. The coverage analysis (annotating <10% of images covers >99% of points, Eq. 3) is a convincing efficiency argument.

Substantial data collection effort: 9 scenes, ~194,000 m^2, 20,160 samples with RGB, semantic voxel grids, and metric depth maps across three altitudes, seasons, and scenario types; class-wise DBSCAN parameters, annotation ratios (Tab. 8), reprojection errors (Tab. 7), and depth statistics are reported in the supplementary.

Useful additional assets: fine-tuned DAv2 metric depth model for the aerial domain with clear quantitative gains over the off-the-shelf metric variant, and a reciprocal cross-domain generalization experiment (Tab. 10).
The paper is honest about several limitations in the conclusion (static scenes, temporal inconsistencies, manual masks) and commits to releasing the dataset.
weaknesses: Ground-truth validity is not independently verified. The entire volumetric ground truth derives from photogrammetric reconstruction plus heuristic densification (visual hull carving, Poisson surface fills, kNN relabeling). The only quantitative quality check is RMS reprojection error (1.24 px), which measures geometric self-consistency of SfM/MVS, not semantic or volumetric accuracy. There is no validation against independently surveyed 3D annotations, no held-out subset with manual voxel-level verification, and no estimate of label-noise rate. Since visual hull and Poisson fill largely hallucinate unobserved interior voxels, systematic bias in the 'completion' targets is plausible and unquantified.

The benchmark results are alarming rather than merely challenging: CGFormer achieves overall mIoU of 0.0097 and IoU of 0.2406 (Tab. 11), with essentially every class at or near 0.000 IoU except Building (0.079). Either the task is ill-posed at this resolution/viewpoint, the evaluation protocol is mismatched, or the labels are too noisy for meaningful learning. The paper frames this as 'existing SSC models fall short,' but with only one method evaluated, near-zero semantics do not establish a usable benchmark; the conclusion that 'CGFormer is well-suited to aerial SSC under near-uniform class distributions' (Sec. 5.2) directly contradicts these numbers and reveals weak result interpretation. The claim of 'near-uniform class distributions' is also contradicted by Tab. 6, where Building alone is 75.7% of voxels.

Benchmark breadth is very thin for a 'benchmark' contribution: only CGFormer is evaluated for SSC. No comparisons with MonoScene, VoxFormer, TPVFormer, Symphonies, or other methods discussed in Sec. 2, so it is impossible to know whether failures are method-specific or dataset-wide, and no baseline numbers exist for future work to compare against.

Dataset diversity is narrower than the framing suggests: a single geographic region, 9 scenes, and complete absence of dynamic objects (explicitly acknowledged) which are arguably the hardest and most important part of aerial scene understanding for autonomous flying.

OccuFly is single-view only while compared terrestrial benchmarks (Occ3D, OpenOccupancy, SSCBench) are multi-view (Tab. 2), making the comparison in Tab. 2 somewhat misleading about relative difficulty and scale; the near-zero results may partly stem from this fundamentally harder input setting rather than dataset quality.

Reproducibility during review is limited: data collection locations are withheld, and no public code or dataset link is provided yet; evaluation depends on a proprietary pipeline (Agisoft Metashape) that reviewers and users cannot inspect or reproduce exactly.

Presentation issues that signal insufficient polish: Sec. 5.2's contradictory claims noted above, typos ('data data generation', 'aquired', 'Paltform' in Tab. 8), 'substantially minimizing' in Sec. 3.1, and qualitative SSC visualizations (Figs. 4, 8) showing fragmented predictions that are hard to reconcile with any positive claim.

strengths: Clear identification of a genuine gap: aerial Semantic Scene Completion is essentially unexplored, and OccuFly is presented as the first real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark, with a well-motivated argument for why LiDAR-centric pipelines are ill-suited to UAV platforms (regulations, payload, sparsity from elevated viewpoints).

The data generation framework (Sec. 3.3) is technically substantive and clearly formalized: SfM+MVS reconstruction, stratified 2D annotation with quantified coverage (Eq. 3, <10% of images cover >99% of points), multi-view label voting, class-aware densification (visual hull carving for instances, Poisson reconstruction for ground), frustum culling, and SemanticKITTI-style invalid/surface/occluded masks. This is a reusable contribution beyond the dataset itself.

The dataset is large and diverse for its domain: 9 scenes, >20,000 samples, 22 classes, ~194,000 m², three altitudes, multiple seasons and scenario types, plus >20,000 metric depth maps — substantially larger than prior low-altitude depth datasets (Tab. 9).

Comprehensive supplementary material: per-scene reprojection errors (Tab. 7), annotation ratios (Tab. 8), implementation hyperparameters, class frequencies/groups, depth histograms, and a cross-domain zero-shot depth experiment (Tab. 10), which strengthens reproducibility and credibility.

Benchmark results are honest and informative: the poor CGFormer performance (mIoU ~0.008, IoU ~0.24) and altitude-wise analysis are reported transparently and used to argue the dataset exposes real challenges rather than being cherry-picked; the fine-tuned DAv2-OccuFly depth model is a useful additional release.
Commitment to public release with SSCBench-compatible formatting lowers adoption barriers for the community.
weaknesses: Benchmark breadth is thin: only a single SSC method (CGFormer) is evaluated, and with fairly modest adaptation (grid resized, 25 epochs, batch size 1). The central claim that 'existing SSC models fall short' in the aerial domain rests on one architecture; results from 2-3 diverse methods (e.g., MonoScene, VoxFormer, TPVFormer) would substantially strengthen the benchmark analysis.

Ground-truth validation is largely indirect. Reprojection RMSE (1.24 px) validates geometric consistency of SfM+MVS, but not semantic label fidelity: majority voting plus two rounds of kNN propagation, visual-hull carving of unobserved interior voxels, and Poisson hole-filling can introduce systematic label noise and hallucinated occupancy. There is no quantitative or human-verified assessment of voxel-level label accuracy against held-out manual annotations.

Task validity concerns: with single nadir/oblique views, a large fraction of the grid is only 'completed' via densification heuristics (visual hulls, Poisson surfaces) rather than truly observed information; the paper does not analyze how much of the completion target is observable vs. synthesized, which affects what the benchmark actually measures.

Geographic and scale diversity is limited: all 9 scenes come from a single region, and collection locations are withheld during review, weakening immediate reproducibility. Extreme class imbalance (Building 75.7% vs. Person 0.0002%) also sits awkwardly with the claim that CGFormer is 'well-suited to aerial SSC under near-uniform class distributions' (Sec. 5.2), which reads as inconsistent with Tab. 6.

The narrative around the poor SSC results is somewhat circular: very low absolute numbers (mIoU ~0.008) could equally indicate benchmark noise, voxel-grid/adaptation mismatch, or training underfitting as domain difficulty; the paper asserts the latter without ablations (e.g., oracle depth, ground-truth-depth inputs, longer training) to disentangle these factors.

Dataset design choices (voxel size 0.5 m, 192×128×128 grid, fixed 22-class taxonomy) are reasonable but not justified against alternatives; the class list mixes very rare classes (Flying Animal, Cable) that are essentially unlearnable at the reported frequencies.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel contribution: OccuFly is presented as the first real-world, camera-based (LiDAR-free) aerial SSC benchmark, addressing a genuine gap — existing SSC datasets (SemanticKITTI, nuScenes, SSCBench, Occ3D) are terrestrial and LiDAR-dependent, and the paper convincingly argues why LiDAR is impractical for UAVs (regulations, mass/energy constraints, sparsity from elevated viewpoints).

The data generation framework is technically well-engineered and clearly formalized: SfM+MVS reconstruction with 2D–3D correspondences, coverage-aware stratified selection of <10% images for manual annotation (coverage ρ(J) > 0.99 of 3D points), multi-view label lifting via majority voting with kNN refinement, and a sensible class-aware densification pipeline (visual-hull carving for instances, Poisson reconstruction for ground classes, direct voxelization otherwise) with a precedence-based aggregation.

Validation of ground-truth quality goes beyond qualitative claims: quantified annotation coverage (Eq. 3), 9.17% average annotation ratio, RMSE reprojection error of 1.24 px, and a 92% pixel-wise agreement check against 135 held-out manual annotations across all scenes/altitudes. The rejection of 2D pseudo-labeling baselines (SAM yields poor aerial results; ConvNeXt-trained pseudo-labels reach only 17.58% mIoU) credibly justifies the manual annotation strategy.

The benchmark experiments are informative rather than decorative: SSC results (DISC 29.52 IoU but only ~2 mIoU) and depth results (zero-shot foundation models fail catastrophically, e.g., MapAnything δ1 = 0.000; fine-tuned DepthAnything2 improves δ1 to 0.834 while SILog slightly degrades) substantiate the claimed domain gap, and altitude-wise analysis in the supplementary adds useful insight.

Good reproducibility practices: SSCBench-compatible data organization, released fine-tuned DepthAnything-v2, detailed supplementary with hyperparameters (DBSCAN parameters per class, kNN settings, Poisson parameters), per-scene statistics, and depth distributions.

The paper is honest about limitations (static scenes only, temporal inconsistencies across altitudes, possibility of pseudo-label automation) in the conclusion, and the framing of these as future research opportunities is appropriate.
weaknesses: Limited geographic and structural diversity relative to the stated ambition: all 9 scenes come from a single region (Ingolstadt, Germany), and the test split contains only 2 scenes (~3,842 samples), which raises concerns about generalization claims and statistical robustness of the reported benchmark numbers. Disjoint geographic splits partially mitigate this, but the dataset is still modest in scene count.

The benchmarked SSC baseline set is narrow: only two methods (Symphonies and DISC), both depth-prior-based. Notably, LiDAR-free methods such as MonoScene are not evaluated, and the extremely low mIoU (~2%) makes it hard to distinguish whether the failure is a fundamental aerial domain gap or a suboptimal adaptation of the two chosen baselines (e.g., hyperparameters, class weighting, or the replacement depth estimator). A per-method tuning sensitivity analysis would strengthen the 'fundamental limitation' claim.

Ground-truth for occluded/completed regions is synthesized via visual-hull carving and Poisson reconstruction, i.e., hallucinated geometry rather than observation. The occluded/surface/invalid masks (following SemanticKITTI) help, but the paper does not quantify how much of the evaluation grid relies on densified (rather than observed) voxels, nor how densification errors (e.g., over-carved hulls for concave objects, Poisson bulging) propagate into label errors. The 92% pixel agreement check evaluates rendering of the semantic point cloud, not the densified voxel grid itself.

Severe class imbalance (Building 62.15%, Person 0.0001%) means the benchmark's mIoU is dominated by a handful of classes, and the class-wise table shows most rare classes are essentially unsolved (all zeros). While this is partly the point of a hard benchmark, the paper could discuss evaluation-metric alternatives or per-class stratification more prominently.

Voxel resolution of 0.5 m is coarser than most terrestrial benchmarks (0.05–0.4 m in Tab. 2), and single-view-only samples limit the multi-view occupancy prediction line of research; these design choices are justified but constrain the benchmark's scope.

Minor presentation issues: heavy reliance on supplementary material for central results (class-wise SSC analysis, altitude-wise depth analysis, annotation ratios), the typos 'Aquired'/'Occufly' in Tab. 9, and Table 2's grid-resolution row for Occ3D-Waymo appears inconsistent, all of which slightly hamper readability.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: no real-world, camera-based SSC benchmark exists for the aerial domain, and the motivation for avoiding LiDAR (UAV payload/energy constraints, flight regulations, sparsity from elevated viewpoints) is well argued (Sec. 1).

The data generation framework is clearly and rigorously formalized (Secs. 3.2–3.3), combining SfM+MVS reconstruction, coverage-driven 2D annotation selection (Eq. 3), multi-view label lifting with kNN refinement, class-aware densification (visual hull carving, Poisson reconstruction), and SemanticKITTI-style frustum culling with invalid/surface/occluded masks.

The annotation-efficiency claim is supported empirically: annotating ~9.17% of images covers >99% of reconstructed points (Tab. 9), and an independent check on 135 held-out annotations reports 92% pixel-wise agreement (Sec. 4.3).

The benchmark evaluation is reasonably broad: two SOTA SSC methods (Symphonies, DISC) and four metric depth foundation models in zero-shot vs. fine-tuned settings, with altitude-wise and class-wise breakdowns in the supplementary (Tabs. 11, 12), substantiating the claimed domain gap.

The dataset is substantial relative to prior aerial depth datasets (20,611 samples, 21 classes, ~194,000 m², multiple altitudes, seasons, and environment types; Tabs. 1–3), and follows SSCBench-style organization for ease of adoption. Reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation parameters (supplementary Sec. 8, Tabs. 6–7).
weaknesses: Ground-truth 'completion' is fundamentally reconstruction-derived: occupancy is obtained by voxelizing the SfM+MVS point cloud (with visual-hull and Poisson densification). This means the 'completed' regions are themselves hallucinations of the reconstruction pipeline, so the benchmark measures agreement with one reconstruction rather than truly observed complete scenes — a methodological caveat that is under-discussed relative to its importance.

Geographic and scene diversity is narrow: all 9 scenes come from a single region (Ingolstadt, Germany), and the train/test splits differ mainly in season/scene rather than geography, weakening claims of a 'robust benchmark' for generalization.

The SSC benchmark results are extremely weak (best mIoU ~2.2%, IoU ~29.5%, Tab. 4), with most classes at 0.00. While this supports the 'domain gap' narrative, it also raises the question of whether the benchmark protocol (e.g., 0.5 m voxels, single-view, severe class imbalance with Building at 62% frequency) is well-matched to existing methods, and whether more methods or protocol variants were explored.

Only two SSC baselines are evaluated; given the coarse resolution (192×128×128 at 0.5 m) and single-view setup, additional or adapted baselines would be needed to establish the benchmark's discriminative value rather than merely showing failure.

The geometric fidelity validation (92% pixel agreement, 1.24 px reprojection error) is partly self-referential — rendering the semantic point cloud and comparing to annotations that share the same underlying reconstruction — so it validates label lifting consistency more than absolute 3D accuracy; no external reference (e.g., surveyed checkpoints or LiDAR cross-check on one scene) is provided.
Static-scene assumption means dynamic objects are suppressed in ground truth (acknowledged only in the conclusion), which limits the benchmark's usefulness for realistic UAV perception.

Several claims are asserted but deferred entirely to the supplementary (class taxonomy details, scene-wise depth distributions, annotation ratios), reducing main-paper self-containedness; the evaluation of DepthAnything3 uses zero-shot only because training scripts are unavailable, making the foundation-model comparison uneven.

Depth Anything2 fine-tuning degrades SILog (0.192 → 0.112 is actually an improvement, but RMSE 28.4 → 4.8 with SILog 0.192 → 0.112 shows the fine-tuned model trades relative accuracy) — the paper glosses over what this trade-off implies about the depth ground truth itself being reconstruction-biased.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated gap: the paper identifies a genuine lack of real-world aerial SSC benchmarks and provides a convincing rationale (flight regulations, mass/energy constraints, LiDAR sparsity from elevated viewpoints) for a camera-based pipeline.

The data generation framework is technically well-specified and scalable: stratified selection of <10% of images for 2D annotation, majority-vote label lifting via 2D-3D correspondences, kNN propagation, and class-aware densification (visual hull carving for instances, Poisson reconstruction for ground) reduce 3D annotation to 2D labeling. The coverage analysis (rho(J) > 0.99 with <10% annotated images) and per-scene annotation statistics in the supplementary are convincing.

Thorough dataset validation: the authors quantify geometric fidelity (1.24 px mean RMS reprojection error, scene-wise in Tab. 8), semantic accuracy (92% pixel agreement on 135 held-out annotations), and rule out cheap 2D pseudo-labeling alternatives (17.58% mIoU with a ConvNeXt aerial baseline), which supports the need for manual annotation.

Meaningful scale and diversity: ~20,600 samples, 194k m2, 21 classes, three altitudes, three environment types, all seasons, with train/val/test splits from disjoint geographic scenes; SSCBench-compatible organization eases adoption. Depth GT (20k+ metric depth maps) also makes it the largest public low-altitude aerial metric depth dataset (Tab. 3).

The benchmark experiments (SSC with Symphonies/DISC; zero-shot vs. fine-tuned metric depth with MapAnything, Metric3Dv2, DepthAnything-v2/v3) are carefully executed with official implementations, and consistently support the claimed domain gap of vision foundation models in aerial settings; altitude-wise and class-wise breakdowns in the supplementary add analytical depth.

Honest discussion of limitations (static scenes, cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies, automation prospects) in the conclusion, plus extensive supplementary material, suggests good reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark results are alarmingly low (mIoU ~0.5-2.2% for both SSC methods across all altitudes). While the authors attribute this to a domain gap, such uniformly poor numbers raise the alternative possibility that the ground truth itself is difficult to learn or noisy (e.g., visual hull carving produces hollow, non-physical instance volumes; Poisson-reconstructed ground may over-smooth; label lifting via kNN introduces boundary noise). The paper does not provide an upper-bound or human-learnability check (e.g., fitting a single scene or oracle-depth variant) to disambiguate domain gap from label-quality issues.

Ground truth derived from MVS reconstruction creates a potential circularity: the depth maps used as geometric priors by DISC/Symphonies come from the same SfM+MVS pipeline that produces the occupancy ground truth, complicating interpretation of both SSC and depth results.

Dataset breadth is limited in important ways: only 9 scenes, all within one geographic region (Ingolstadt, Germany), single-camera views, and only 2 validation / 2 test scenes; with extreme class imbalance (Building ~62-75% of voxels, several classes <0.01%), test-set variance on rare classes is high.

Only two SSC methods are benchmarked, both terrestrial-designed with depth-prior back-projection; no aerial-adapted or LiDAR-free lightweight baselines, and no fine-tuning of SSC methods on OccuFly, leaving open whether the low SSC numbers reflect irreducible difficulty or suboptimal adaptation of the benchmarks' hyperparameters (e.g., voxel grid resolution 192x128x128 at 0.5 m differs substantially from the terrestrial setups these methods were tuned for).

The static-scene assumption suppresses dynamic objects entirely (the paper's own conclusion notes this), which weakens the claim of a complete SSC benchmark for downstream UAV navigation; similarly, nadir/oblique mixing and cross-altitude frustum culling from later captures introduce acknowledged temporal inconsistencies.

The dataset occupies a coarse voxel resolution (0.5 m) compared to e.g. Occ3D (0.05-0.4 m), limiting fine-grained aerial reasoning (small objects like persons/cranes occupy few voxels and are essentially undetectable per Tab. 11).

Methodological novelty is modest: SfM+MVS, majority-vote label lifting, kNN, visual hull carving, and Poisson reconstruction are all established components; the contribution is their composition and adaptation, which is acceptable for a benchmark paper but should not be oversold.

Depth experiments have asymmetries that slightly weaken conclusions: MapAnything cannot be fine-tuned and DepthAnything3 lacks training scripts, so fine-tuning is only demonstrated for DepthAnything2 (and with a ViT-Small variant), and the SILog regression after fine-tuning is only briefly addressed.
